16 A bead is released from rest at point P and slides along a wire, as shown.
P
NOT TO
SCALE
1.4 m s–1
Q
h
40 cm
The track loops around and forms a vertical circle of diameter 40 cm. At point Q, the bead has a
speed of 1.4 m s–1.
Air resistance and friction on the wire are negligible.
What is the height h from which the bead is released?
A
0.30 m
B
0.40 m
C
0.50 m
D
0.60 m

hints: Notice point Q is at the top of the loop, so its height above the bottom datum is the full diameter $40 \text{ cm} = 0.40 \text{ m}$, while P starts from rest at height $h$.
With friction negligible, total mechanical energy is conserved, so the initial $mgh$ at P equals $mg \times 0.40$ plus $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$ at Q with $v = 1.4 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Cancel $m$ and solve $gh = g \times 0.40 + v^2/2$ for $h$, remembering to convert $40 \text{ cm}$ to metres before adding the $v^2/(2g)$ term.
walkthrough: Take the bottom of the track as gravitational potential energy zero. At P the bead is at rest, so total energy is $E_P = mgh$.
At Q the bead is $0.40 \text{ m}$ above the datum and moving, so total energy is $E_Q = mg \times 0.40 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2$ with $v = 1.4 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
With no friction or air resistance, $E_P = E_Q$, so $mgh = mg \times 0.40 + \frac{1}{2}mv^2$. Cancel $m$ to get $gh = g \times 0.40 + v^2/2$.
The kinetic term is $0.10 \text{ m}$, so $h = 0.40 + 0.10 = 0.50 \text{ m}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: 0.30 m is below the 0.40 m height of Q, so the bead could not gain enough gravitational potential energy to reach Q.

B.explanation: 0.40 m equals the height of Q, which would leave zero kinetic energy at Q, but the bead has speed $1.4 \text{ m s}^{-1}$ there.

C.explanation: Conservation gives $h = 0.40 + v^2/(2g) = 0.50 \text{ m}$, which provides both the potential energy at Q and the observed kinetic energy.

D.explanation: 0.60 m gives too much total energy and would predict a speed at Q greater than $1.4 \text{ m s}^{-1}$.
